knowledge_point.title: Finding the Slope of the Tangent at a Point of a Function Involving Reciprocal Trigonometric Functions

question.:question/problem: Find the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\sqrt{3}$ if $f(x)=16\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x+\frac{1}{x}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we calculate the derivative using the sum rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(16\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x+\frac{1}{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(16\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x+{x}^{-1}) \\  & =16(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =-16\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $x=\sqrt{3}$ in the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\sqrt{3}) & =-16\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(\sqrt{3})\operatorname{tan}⁡(\sqrt{3})-\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}} \\  & =-16\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(\sqrt{3})\operatorname{tan}⁡(\sqrt{3})-\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
